(4)

parts.text:

(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: $2^6=64$ (award when first seen, not $64x^0$)
M1: Attempt binomial expansion with correct structure for at least one term of the form $\binom{6}{p}\times(2)^{6-p}(-5x)^p$ with $p=1$ or $p=2$ consistently. Condone sign errors. Condone missing brackets if later work implies correct structure and allow alternative forms for binomial coefficients e.g. $^6C_1$ or $\binom{6}{1}$
A1: $-960x$ (not $+-960x$)
A1: $(+)6000x^2$
Way 2: B1: $64(1\pm...)$ — 64 and $(1\pm...)$ award when first seen. M1: Correct structure for at least one of the underlined terms, e.g. a term of the form $\binom{6}{p}\times(kx)^p$ with $p=1$ or $p=2$ consistently and $k\neq\pm5$. Condone sign errors. Condone missing brackets if later work implies correct structure but it must be an expansion of $(1-kx)^6$ where $k\neq\pm5$. A1: $-960x$ (not $+-960x$). A1: $(+)6000x^2$

- $+6\times(2)^5(-5x)+\frac{6\times5}{2}(2)^4(-5x)^2$ M1

- Way 2: $\left(1-\frac{5x}{2}\right)^6=1-6\times\frac{5x}{2}+\frac{6\times5}{2}\left(-\frac{5x}{2}\right)^2$ M1

questions.stem:
f$(x) = ax^3+bx^2-4x-3$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants.
Given that $(x-1)$ is a factor of f$(x)$,

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) show that $a+b=7$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Attempt f$(\pm1)$: f$(1)=a+b-4-3=0$ or $a+b-7=0$
A1: $a+b=7$* (Must be f(1) and =0 needs to be seen)
Long Division alt: M1: $(ax^3+bx^2-4x-3)\div(x-1)=ax^2+px+q$ where $p$ and $q$ are in terms of $a$ or $b$ or both and sets their remainder $=0$ (NB Quotient $=ax^2+(a+b)x+(a+b-4)$)
A1: $a+b=7$*

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Given also that, when f$(x)$ is divided by $(x+2)$, the remainder is 9,
(b) find the value of $a$ and the value of $b$, showing each step in your working.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Attempt f$(-2)$ and uses f$(-2)=9$: f$(-2)=a(-2)^3+b(-2)^2-4(-2)-3=9$
A1: $-8a+4b+8-3=9$ (correct equation with exponents of $(-2)$ removed) i.e. $(-8a+4b=4)$
M1: Solves the given equation from part (a) and their equation in $a$ and $b$ from part (b) as far as $a=...$ or $b=...$
A1: $a=2$ and $b=5$ (both correct)
Long Division alt: M1: $(ax^3+bx^2-4x-3)\div(x+2)=ax^2+px+q$ where $p$ and $q$ are in terms of $a$ or $b$ or both and sets their remainder $=9$ (NB Quotient $=ax^2+(b-2a)x+(4a-4-2b)$)
A1: $4b-8a+5=9$. Follow scheme for final 2 marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text:

parts.text:

questions.stem: The circle $C$ has equation $x^2+y^2-20x-24y+195=0$ The centre of $C$ is at the point $M$.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find
(i) the coordinates of the point $M$,
(ii) the radius of the circle $C$.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: $x=10$
B1: $y=12$
M1: Uses $(x-10)^2+(y-12)^2=-195+100+144\Rightarrow r=...$ Completes the square for both $x$ and $y$ in an attempt to find $r$. Completes the square for both $x$ and $y$: $(x\pm\text{"10"})^2\pm a$ and $(y\pm\text{"12"})^2\pm b+195=0$, $(a,b\neq0)$. Allow errors in obtaining their $r^2$ but must find square root
A1: $r=\sqrt{10^2+12^2-195}$ (a correct numerical expression for $r$ including the square root and can be implied by a correct value for $r$)
A1: $r=7$ (not $r=\pm7$ unless $-7$ is rejected)
Way 2: B1: $x=10$, B1: $y=12$ — Compares the given equation with $x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0$ to write down centre $(-g,-f)$ i.e. $(10,12)$
M1: Uses $r=\sqrt{(\pm\text{"10"})^2+(\pm\text{"12"})^2-c}$
A1: $r=\sqrt{10^2+12^2-195}$ (a correct numerical expression for $r$)
A1: $r=7$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
$N$ is the point with coordinates $(25, 32)$.
(b) Find the length of the line $MN$.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Correct use of Pythagoras: $MN=\sqrt{(25-\text{"10"})^2+(32-\text{"12"})^2}$
A1: $MN(=\sqrt{625})=25$

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The tangent to $C$ at a point $P$ on the circle passes through point $N$.
(c) Find the length of the line $NP$.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: $NP=\sqrt{(\text{"25"}^2-\text{"7"}^2)}$ i.e. $NP=\sqrt{MN^2-r^2}$
A1: $NP(=\sqrt{576})=24$
Way 2: M1: Correct strategy for finding $NP$: $\cos(NMP)=\frac{7}{\text{"25"}}\Rightarrow NP=\text{"25"}\sin(NMP)$
A1: $NP=24$

The finite region $R$, as shown in Figure 2, is bounded by the $x$-axis and the curve with equation
$y=27-2x-9\sqrt{x}-\frac{16}{x^2}$, $x>0$
The curve crosses the $x$-axis at the points $(1,0)$ and $(4,0)$.

parts.label: a

$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 1 & 1.5 & 2 & 2.5 & 3 & 3.5 & 4\\ \hline y & 0 & 5.866 & & 5.210 & & 1.856 & 0\\ \hline\end{array}$
(2)

parts.label: b
parts.text:

(4)

(6)
